chapters.title: Opening
chapters.subtitle: Welcome and course prerequisites
chapters.heading: Build a system you can explain
chapters.description: Welcome to Containers in Practice. We will start with a small Node.js application and its API, package it into an OCI image, then explore what changes when that workload scales, fails, and needs stronger boundaries.
paragraphs: You do not need container or Kubernetes experience to begin. If Git is new to you, the short primer will help you keep track of your experiments. We will introduce each tool when its purpose becomes clear.

Before the first build, we will check your workstation. Later modules run a local Kubernetes cluster alongside application and data services. A quick check of memory, disk space, and virtualization now will help us distinguish a workload problem from a machine that has run out of room.
Work through the course at your own pace: listen or read, study the system, then investigate in your terminal. Each checkpoint asks you to keep evidence of what happened and explain what it proves.
chapters.insight: The goal is a working system—and a clear account of why it works.
chapters.evidence: Know the course path and the environment you will use before installing the lab toolchain.
chapters.proof: Identify your operating-system path and one workstation property to verify in Module 0.

baseline.question: Can your computer support the labs before you install anything?
baseline.explore: Use the workstation sizing table and resource check in Opening, Module −0.1. Record logical CPU count, RAM, free storage and virtualization support; compare host and Linux guest allocations if applicable.
baseline.observe: A recorded machine baseline and a realistic plan for the Kubernetes modules, not merely installed tools.
baseline.confusion: My laptop has enough RAM but the Linux guest shows less.
baseline.recover: WSL and Lima are resource-limited virtual environments. Check guest allocation independently of host capacity, and reduce workloads or reserve more resources before scaling labs.

toolchain.question: Which tool solves which problem?
toolchain.explore: Choose your operating system in the installation guide. Install and verify the six tools. Leave Kubernetes for Module 2.
toolchain.observe: Six distinct responsibilities without six unrelated installation exercises.
toolchain.confusion: A command is missing or a package is unavailable.
toolchain.recover: Choose your operating system in the installation guide. Check the package manager response and confirm you are in the named terminal. RHEL may require enabled repositories.

preflight.question: Does the runtime execute an image?
preflight.explore: Compare the output of `podman --version` with the output of the Podman hello image. Which proves execution?
preflight.observe: An image is downloaded, a process runs, and it exits successfully.
preflight.confusion: The version command works but the image fails.
preflight.recover: Separate registry/network failures from rootless runtime failures; preserve the error before reinstalling anything.

recovery.question: What failed before you changed anything?
recovery.explore: Write the first failing command, exact error, and last known-good output before attempting a repair.
recovery.observe: A falsifiable hypothesis rather than a vague “it broke.”
recovery.recover: Compare only one variable at a time. Reset after you have captured enough evidence to explain the failure.

learning-modes.question: How much work demonstrates mastery?
learning-modes.explore: Choose Core for the proof, Deep Dive for understanding a mechanism, or Challenge for independent implementation.
learning-modes.observe: An outcome you can verify—not a checklist of pages visited.
learning-modes.recover: Return to the stated checkpoint. Optional depth should never block forward progress.

checkpoint.question: Is your environment ready for someone else to reproduce it?
checkpoint.explore: Capture the tool versions and a successful container run, then tag Checkpoint 0. Before moving on, name which parts of the upcoming application belong in its image and which belong outside it.
checkpoint.observe: One verified baseline plus a clear distinction between image, runtime configuration, and persistent data.
checkpoint.confusion: Unsure whether the checkpoint is complete or what Module 1 will change.
checkpoint.recover: Verify an OCI container actually runs—not just that a version command responds. Then use the next-module handoff below to preview what becomes reproducible.

m1-opening.question: What does “works on my machine” hide?
m1-opening.explore: Identify three assumptions outside the source code: ports, database location, or environment configuration.
m1-opening.observe: A system boundary that can be expressed and tested.
m1-opening.confusion: The API works; why package it?
m1-opening.recover: Running once is not the goal. Someone else should be able to reconstruct it from source and declared configuration.

inspect.question: Which parts of the API need a database?
inspect.explore: Compare the health endpoint with the records endpoints. Determine which dependencies each request exercises.
inspect.observe: A healthy HTTP response does not prove database connectivity.
inspect.confusion: The health endpoint succeeds but records fail.
inspect.recover: Inspect the DB host, port, connection error, and whether Postgres-QL is actually reachable.

image.question: Which settings survive image reuse?
image.explore: Use the same image to start a replacement container. Observe which settings changed without rebuilding.
image.observe: The artifact and the running instance are distinct.
image.confusion: Image build succeeds, but published port fails.
image.recover: Inspect the port mapping and which interface the application binds inside the container.

config.question: Can one image run in two environments?
config.explore: Change an environment variable at start-up without changing the image digest.
config.observe: Environment-specific behavior with an unchanged artifact.
config.confusion: Changing an env var has no effect.
config.recover: Confirm which variable the application reads and whether a newly started process received it.

network.question: What does the database hostname resolve to?
network.explore: Compare name resolution and published ports inside and outside the Podman network.
network.observe: Containers communicate through their network identity, not the host’s localhost assumption.
network.confusion: `localhost` works on the host but not in the API container.
network.recover: Inside a container, localhost points to that container. Check the network name and database service hostname.

storage.question: What survives deleting an API container?
storage.explore: Create a record, replace the API container, and look for the same record. Compare data storage with compute lifecycle.
storage.observe: Data survives because its storage is independent of the disposable container filesystem.
storage.confusion: A volume exists, so the data must be backed up.
storage.recover: A volume preserves data across container replacement; it does not guarantee a recoverable backup.

harden.question: What is actually inside your image?
harden.explore: Inspect installed packages, build layers, and the user identity used by the runtime.
harden.observe: An explicit reason for removing or retaining each runtime dependency.
harden.confusion: A smaller image seems automatically safer.
harden.recover: Size alone is not a security conclusion. Check privileges, dependencies, and configuration as well.

iac.question: Can configuration replace shell history?
iac.explore: Compare the intended resources in the OpenTofu plan with what exists after applying it.
iac.observe: Reviewable intended state and explainable changes.
iac.confusion: A plan and a running infrastructure look identical.
iac.recover: A plan describes proposed action. Observe after apply to verify resources actually exist.

rebuild.question: Did you reconstruct or merely restart?
rebuild.explore: Remove disposable containers and recreate them from the declared configuration, then re-test the API.
rebuild.observe: A working system restored from source and configuration, not memory.
rebuild.confusion: A deleted container also removed important data.
rebuild.recover: Stop and check which storage location holds persistent data before retrying the rebuild.

challenge.question: Same artifact, different environment?
challenge.explore: Deploy the same image in two named configurations; compare image identity and environment values.
challenge.observe: Both behave correctly without separate rebuilds.
challenge.confusion: Configuration is baked into the image.
challenge.recover: Find values supplied during build that belong at launch or deployment instead.

conclusion.question: What evidence would convince a teammate?
conclusion.explore: Summarize image identity, configuration location, database persistence, and reconstruction commands.
conclusion.observe: A reproducible handoff another engineer can verify.
conclusion.confusion: Your notes contain only successful command screenshots.
conclusion.recover: Add what you expected, what you observed, and how to recover if a step fails.

m2-opening.question: Is reproducible the same as scalable?
m2-opening.explore: Follow the path of one request. Predict what breaks when demand exceeds the capacity of one API instance.
m2-opening.observe: A specific bottleneck hypothesis rather than an assumed 3× improvement.
m2-opening.confusion: A Service sounds like an application server.
m2-opening.recover: A Service gives a stable endpoint; its networking dataplane forwards traffic to eligible Pods.

m2-baseline.question: What will you compare after scaling?
m2-baseline.explore: Pick throughput, latency, and error rate. State the load conditions so you can repeat them after the architecture changes.
m2-baseline.observe: A baseline measured before adding replicas.
m2-baseline.confusion: Many requests sent must mean high throughput.
m2-baseline.recover: Count successful requests completed per second; attempted load and delivered throughput are different.

m2-replicas.question: What actually forwards client connections?
m2-replicas.explore: Trace Clients → Service → eligible API Pods. Inspect which ready endpoints the Service can reach.
m2-replicas.observe: Different Pods can serve independent connections through the same stable endpoint.
m2-replicas.confusion: Every HTTP request must go to a different Pod.
m2-replicas.recover: Kubernetes Service routing is generally at the connection/flow level; persistent HTTP connections can reuse a backend.

m2-shared-state.question: How can Pod 3 read a value written by Pod 1?
m2-shared-state.explore: Watch the animation. The first request writes a preference through Pod 1; a later connection reaches Pod 3 and reads the same value.
m2-shared-state.observe: Shared state is available independently of the Pod that originally handled the request.
m2-shared-state.confusion: Every request appears to hit Valkey.
m2-shared-state.recover: Only requests needing state access Valkey. A health request can be answered entirely by an API Pod.

m2-resources.question: Which resource does the scheduler reserve?
m2-resources.explore: Compare a CPU request with a CPU limit and predict how throttling differs from an out-of-memory termination.
m2-resources.observe: Scheduling, throttling, and memory failure are distinct outcomes.
m2-resources.confusion: CPU utilization means host CPU consumption.
m2-resources.recover: For HPA resource utilization, usage is compared with the declared workload CPU request.

m2-load.question: Did the change really improve user experience?
m2-load.explore: Repeat the same load profile through the Kubernetes Service and compare p95 latency, successful throughput, and errors.
m2-load.observe: A before-and-after claim supported by comparable measurements.
m2-load.confusion: CPU appears healthy but requests are slow.
m2-load.recover: Look downstream at database response time, connection queues, and per-request work.

m2-hpa.question: When will Kubernetes add a replica?
m2-hpa.explore: Observe actual CPU use relative to requests, the HPA target, and the time until a new Pod becomes ready.
m2-hpa.observe: An autoscaler decision with observable scheduling and readiness delay.
m2-hpa.confusion: The replica count does not change immediately.
m2-hpa.recover: Check Metrics Server availability, workload CPU requests, stabilization, and whether load persists.

m2-bottleneck.question: What happens when the database is saturated?
m2-bottleneck.explore: Increase load while examining API latency, datastore operations, and database connection pressure.
m2-bottleneck.observe: Evidence of a limit outside the API replica count.
m2-bottleneck.confusion: More API Pods made performance worse.
m2-bottleneck.recover: Each new Pod may increase load on shared dependencies; identify the limiting service before scaling again.

m2-checkpoint.question: What would convince a reviewer that scaling works?
m2-checkpoint.explore: Present a baseline, a change in replica count, a repeat test, shared-state evidence, and a known limit.
m2-checkpoint.observe: A defensible architecture and performance conclusion.
m2-checkpoint.confusion: You can report success but not explain how you measured it.
m2-checkpoint.recover: Record test method, traffic path, and actual Pod responses; avoid treating replica count itself as proof.

m3-0.question: If an API Pod disappears, which parts of the system can actually recover?
m3-0.explore: Sketch three failure consequences: an interrupted request, a replacement Pod, and an unavailable datastore.
m3-0.observe: The Pod controller may restore the desired replica count, but application success and data safety require separate evidence.
m3-0.confusion: All Pods show Ready. Does that prove the application recovered?
m3-0.recover: Compare requests and database behavior from the client perspective. Ready is one signal, not a complete recovery test.

m3-1.question: What state disappears with a Pod—and what should survive?
m3-1.explore: Before removing anything, identify which values come from the image, environment, process memory, and persistent storage.
m3-1.observe: Replacement restores code and configuration, but not arbitrary writes in a disposable container layer.
m3-1.confusion: The Pod returned to Running; I expected all state to return too.
m3-1.recover: Separate memory, writable layers, ephemeral volumes, and PersistentVolumeClaims. Compare where the record was stored.

m3-2.question: If the database Pod moves, where is its data actually stored?
m3-2.explore: Trace the relationship: database container → mounted volume → claim → volume → underlying storage.
m3-2.observe: A claim may be rebound to a replacement workload, but local storage remains vulnerable to loss of its backing node.
m3-2.confusion: A bound PersistentVolumeClaim means the data is highly available.
m3-2.recover: Inspect the StorageClass, provisioner, access mode, reclaim policy, and physical backing. Bound is not the same as redundant.

m3-3.question: What evidence shows that the backup can restore useful data?
m3-3.explore: Design a disposable target database and a known record-count check. Predict what a backup cannot undo about a subsequent bad write.
m3-3.observe: Restored data is independently queryable and meets an explicitly stated expected result.
m3-3.confusion: A dump file exists; should I call the backup successful?
m3-3.recover: Treat a file as unverified until it is restored to a separate environment and inspected. Check dump format and tool compatibility.

m3-4.question: When should Kubernetes remove a Pod from traffic instead of restarting it?
m3-4.explore: Predict behavior for three conditions: slow startup, temporary database failure, and unrecoverable deadlock.
m3-4.observe: Probe outcomes lead to different actions. Readiness failure and liveness failure are not interchangeable.
m3-4.confusion: A readiness failure restarts the container.
m3-4.recover: Readiness does not, by itself, restart the container. Examine probe type, events, and configured thresholds.

m3-5.question: What happens to a request that is in flight when its Pod begins terminating?
m3-5.explore: Compare a short request, a long-running request, and an abrupt kill. Predict which ones can finish in the grace period.
m3-5.observe: SIGTERM handling, grace period, and endpoint removal coordinate imperfectly; existing connections may still need to finish.
m3-5.confusion: When a Pod is Terminating, no client can still reach it.
m3-5.recover: Consider open connections and delayed convergence; inspect endpoint conditions and app signal handling.

m3-6.question: How can a new release fail without taking the whole Service down?
m3-6.explore: Predict the rollout when new Pods stay unready. Observe the relationship between desired replicas, available replicas, and revision history.
m3-6.observe: New Pods gain eligibility only after readiness succeeds; rollback requires behavioral verification.
m3-6.confusion: A successful rollout undo also restores old database contents.
m3-6.recover: Rollbacks change the Deployment Pod template; they do not automatically reverse schema migrations or restore deleted data.

m3-7.question: What failure would best reveal a weakness in the system?
m3-7.explore: Choose a fault and a prediction, then list evidence from the client, controller, and datastore points of view.
m3-7.observe: A causal explanation: which condition changed, how it was detected, and how recovery was independently verified.
m3-7.confusion: Deleting a Pod proves that the cluster is highly available.
m3-7.recover: A single-node cluster can show controller-level recovery, but cannot prove node or storage high availability.

m3-8.question: Could another engineer reproduce your failure and verify the recovery?
m3-8.explore: Assemble five artifacts: failure hypothesis, baseline, observation, recovery action, and independent functional verification.
m3-8.observe: An evidence-backed claim that identifies exactly which failure modes the lab did—and did not—test.
m3-8.confusion: The replicas are Ready, so I can mark Checkpoint 3 complete.
m3-8.recover: Add a client-side functional test, the restored record validation, and precise limits of the local cluster.

glossary.Container: A running process with isolated views of resources. It shares a kernel rather than bringing a full guest operating system.
glossary.Image: A packaged filesystem and metadata used to start containers. The image and a running instance have different lifecycles.
glossary.OCI: Open Container Initiative: specifications for container images, runtimes, and distribution.
glossary.Pod: The smallest deployable Kubernetes unit. Its containers share networking and can share declared storage.
glossary.Deployment: A Kubernetes controller that manages replicated Pods and rollout updates.
glossary.Service: A stable network endpoint backed by selected, eligible Pod endpoints.
glossary.Cluster: The control plane and worker nodes that run Kubernetes workloads.
glossary.Node: A machine in a cluster that runs Pods. kind uses local container-based nodes for practice.
glossary.Namespace: A scope for many Kubernetes resources. It is not complete security isolation by itself.
glossary.Replica: Another instance of a workload. More replicas help only when the bottleneck can be distributed.
glossary.Volume: Storage mounted into a container. Its lifetime depends on the volume type and underlying storage.
glossary.Readiness: Whether a Pod should be eligible to receive Service traffic.
glossary.Liveness: A probe used to decide whether a container needs restarting.
glossary.Git: Version control that records changes locally and helps people exchange them. Git and GitHub are different things.
glossary.Commit: A recorded snapshot of tracked changes in a Git repository.
glossary.Repository: The files and version history for a project.
glossary.Rootless: A container engine running without root on the host. This does not prove the application process inside a container is non-root.
glossary.Digest: A content identity for an image. A mutable tag is a convenient name, not the same guarantee.
glossary.SBOM: Software Bill of Materials: an inventory of detected software components, not a safety certificate.
glossary.Kubernetes: An open-source system that schedules and manages containerized workloads across a cluster.
glossary.kubectl: The command-line tool used to communicate with a Kubernetes cluster’s API.
glossary.PostgreSQL: An open-source relational database used in this course’s persistence and recovery investigations.
